lead: A vehicle speed loop compares reference and measured speed and commands tractive force. A PI controller removes steady-state speed error; a PD controller adds damping. The vehicle is modelled as a first-order lag, so two gains and one time constant describe the loop. Cruise control, electric-vehicle torque control and ADAS speed tracking use this. Only a few universities teach the tuning method here.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.2 for the cruise loop, and first-order lag plus Laplace transforms from a control course.

sections.h3: Plant, PI law and lambda tuning

blocks.where: m is mass (kg); v is speed (m/s); F is tractive force (N); b is resistance (N per m/s).

blocks.text: Rearranged, τ dv/dt + v = K F, with τ = m/b in s and K = 1/b in (m/s)/N. In Laplace form, V(s)/F(s) = K/(τs + 1).

Error e = v<sub>ref</sub> − v, with v<sub>ref</sub> the wanted speed. PI law: u = K<sub>p</sub> e + K<sub>i</sub> ∫e dt, where u is commanded force (N), K<sub>p</sub> is N per (m/s), and K<sub>i</sub> is N/m (newton per metre of integrated speed error; K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>). Proportional action alone leaves an offset. At steady state K<sub>p</sub>(v<sub>ref</sub> − v) = b v, so e<sub>ss</sub> = b v<sub>ref</sub>/(K<sub>p</sub> + b). For K<sub>p</sub> much larger than b this is close to b v<sub>ref</sub>/K<sub>p</sub>. The integral supplies the force and drives e to zero.

Lambda tuning chooses the closed-loop time constant λ and cancels the plant pole with the PI zero: K<sub>p</sub> = τ/(K λ), T<sub>i</sub> = τ, K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>. Smaller λ gives faster response but larger force, so check actuator saturation. A reference model filters v<sub>ref</sub>, often as 1/(λs + 1), before the loop sees it. On a real vehicle with a rate-limited actuator this slows the demanded force and limits saturation and overshoot; in the ideal first-order loop modelled here the loop already has no overshoot, so the main gain is a smooth force command.

PD law u = K<sub>p</sub> e + K<sub>d</sub> de/dt, where K<sub>d</sub> is N per (m/s²). The derivative predicts error growth and opposes fast speed change, adding damping. With constant v<sub>ref</sub>, de/dt = −dv/dt, so derivative on measurement is u = K<sub>p</sub> e − K<sub>d</sub> dv/dt. This avoids a kick when v<sub>ref</sub> steps.

Measured speed carries sensor noise. A raw derivative amplifies it, so filter the derivative with time constant T<sub>f</sub>, or use a small K<sub>d</sub>. The derivative path becomes s/(T<sub>f</sub> s + 1): a first-order lag with time constant T<sub>f</sub> (in s) on the derivative. PI plus reference model is common for speed; PD alone cannot remove offset because at steady state de/dt = 0. Full Bode and root-locus design belongs to a control course.

For a step in v<sub>ref</sub>, the reference filter turns the jump into a smooth rise before the PI block sees it. Worked example 2 puts numbers on it: the 2500 N jump in force disappears and the peak acceleration falls from 1.67 to 0.61 m/s².

figure.caption: The speed loop of the worked example and its response when the reference steps from 25 to 30 m/s. Lambda tuning gives a first-order rise with λ = 3 s; the reference model makes the start gentler, and neither curve overshoots.

spec.aria: Block diagram from v ref through a summing point, PI block and car block back to the summing point; below, two rising curves of speed against time reaching 28.16 and 26.32 metres per second at 3 seconds and levelling at 30.

examples.question: A 1500 kg vehicle has resistance b = 100 N per m/s. (a) Find K and τ. (b) Choose λ = 3 s and find K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>. (c) With v<sub>ref</sub> = 30 m/s, find the steady error if only proportional action is used.
steps: T<sub>i</sub> = τ = 15 s; K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub> = 500/15 = 33.3 N/m.

Proportional only: at steady state the force K<sub>p</sub> e must balance the resistance b v, so 500(30 − v) = 100v, v = 15000 ÷ 600 = 25 m/s and e = 5 m/s. This is e<sub>ss</sub> = b v<sub>ref</sub> ÷ (K<sub>p</sub> + b) = 3000 ÷ 600. With PI the integral supplies the 2500 N at zero error, so the error falls to zero.
examples.answer: K = 0.01 (m/s)/N, τ = 15 s, K<sub>p</sub> = 500 N/(m/s), T<sub>i</sub> = 15 s, K<sub>i</sub> = 33.3 N/m; proportional-only offset 5 m/s (the car settles at 25 m/s).
examples.check:
m = 1500.0
b = 100.0
K = 1.0 / b
tau = m / b
lam = 3.0
Kp = tau / (K * lam)
Ti = tau
Ki = Kp / Ti
v_ref = 30.0
v_ss = Kp * v_ref / (Kp + b)
e_ss = v_ref - v_ss
print(f'{K:.2f}')
print(f'{tau:.0f}')
print(f'{Kp:.0f}')
print(f'{Ki:.1f}')
print(f'{e_ss:.0f}')
print(f'{v_ss:.0f}')

examples.question: The car of worked example 1 cruises at 25 m/s under the PI loop (K<sub>p</sub> = 500 N/(m/s), T<sub>i</sub> = 15 s), so the integral holds the 2500 N that resistance needs. The driver raises v<sub>ref</sub> to 30 m/s in one step. (a) Find the force and acceleration just after the step. (b) Find the speed after 3 s and 9 s. (c) Repeat with a reference model 1/(3s + 1) on v<sub>ref</sub>, and compare the peak acceleration.
steps: With T<sub>i</sub> = τ the PI zero cancels the plant pole: loop gain = K<sub>p</sub> K ÷ (τ s) = 500 × 0.01 ÷ (15 s) = 1 ÷ (3 s), so the closed loop is 1 ÷ (3s + 1), first order with λ = 3 s.
(a) Just after the step e = 5 m/s while the integral still holds 2500 N: F = 2500 + 500 × 5 = 5000 N. Net force 5000 − 100 × 25 = 2500 N, so a = 2500 ÷ 1500 = 1.67 m/s².
(c) The filtered reference rises as 25 + 5(1 − e<sup>−t/3</sup>), so the error and the force do not jump at t = 0. Speed now follows two lags in series: v(t) = 25 + 5[1 − (1 + t/3)e<sup>−t/3</sup>].
Acceleration dv/dt = 5(t/9)e<sup>−t/3</sup> peaks at t = 3 s: 5 ÷ (3e) = 0.61 m/s², against 1.67 m/s² at once without the model. The peak force falls from 5000 N to about 3550 N.
examples.answer: Without the model: 5000 N and 1.67 m/s² at once, 28.16 m/s at 3 s and 29.75 m/s at 9 s. With it: no jump, 26.32 m/s at 3 s, 29.00 m/s at 9 s, peak acceleration 0.61 m/s² and peak force about 3550 N. Neither overshoots.
examples.check:
import math
v=lambda t:25+5*(1-math.exp(-t/3)); w=lambda t:25+5*(1-(1+t/3)*math.exp(-t/3))
print(v(3),v(9),w(3),w(9),5/(3*math.e))
print(max(100*w(t/100)+1500*5*(t/100/9)*math.exp(-t/300) for t in range(0,3000)))

traps: Error sign: e = v<sub>ref</sub> − v, not v − v<sub>ref</sub>.
K<sub>p</sub> alone leaves a steady offset; the integral term removes it.
Derivative on noisy measured speed amplifies noise; filter it.
Units: K<sub>p</sub> N per m/s; K<sub>i</sub> N/m; K<sub>d</sub> N per (m/s²).
Too small λ demands huge force and saturates the actuator.

quiz.q: State the PI speed law and define K<sub>p</sub>, K<sub>i</sub> and e.
quiz.a: u = K<sub>p</sub> e + K<sub>i</sub> ∫e dt; e = v<sub>ref</sub> − v; K<sub>p</sub> is N per (m/s); K<sub>i</sub> is N/m (K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub>).

quiz.q: Why does integral action remove steady-state speed error?
quiz.a: At steady state the integral holds whatever force is needed, so the error can fall to zero; proportional action alone would need a nonzero error.

quiz.q: For m = 1200 kg, b = 120 N per m/s and λ = 4 s, find K, τ, K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>i</sub>.
A PD loop uses raw measured speed and the signal is noisy. What happens, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: The derivative amplifies noise and the force chatters. Filter the derivative or use derivative on measurement with small K<sub>d</sub>.

quiz.q: K<sub>p</sub> = 400 N per (m/s), b = 80 N per (m/s) and v<sub>ref</sub> = 30 m/s, with proportional action only. Find the steady speed and the error.
quiz.a: 400(30 − v) = 80v, so v = 12000 ÷ 480 = 25 m/s and e = 5 m/s, which is b v<sub>ref</sub> ÷ (K<sub>p</sub> + b) = 2400 ÷ 480. The shortcut b v<sub>ref</sub> ÷ K<sub>p</sub> = 6 m/s overstates it.

quiz.q: What does a reference model do before the PI loop?
quiz.a: It filters v<sub>ref</sub>, often as 1/(λs + 1), so the loop sees a smooth setpoint instead of a step. On real vehicles this limits actuator saturation and gives a smooth force command; in the ideal first-order loop modelled here it does not lower overshoot.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, speed loops run in software at a fixed sample rate, with anti-windup and feedforward from road grade. EV torque control schedules gains because mass and τ change with load. Reference models appear in adaptive cruise and robot velocity control. Search: lambda tuning, derivative on measurement, anti-windup, feedforward speed control.
